blocks.text: Imagine you're organizing a party and need to count the number of ways to arrange guests, choose food, and set up activities without listing every possibility. How can you efficiently determine the total number of configurations?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we'll explore fundamental counting principles that allow us to determine the number of ways to arrange or select items without exhaustive enumeration. These principles form the basis for more advanced topics in complexity and probability.

blocks.title: Sum Rule
blocks.text: The sum rule states that if there are $n_1$ ways to do something and $n_2$ ways to do another thing, and these two actions cannot be done simultaneously, then there are $n_1 + n_2$ ways to choose one of these actions.

blocks.title: Product Rule
blocks.text: The product rule states that if there are $n_1$ ways to do one thing and $n_2$ ways to do another thing after that, then there are $n_1 \times n_2$ ways to perform both actions in sequence.

blocks.title: Applying the Product Rule
blocks.prompt: Suppose you have 3 shirts and 2 pairs of pants. How many different outfits can you create?

steps.text: Identify the number of choices for each item. There are 3 choices for shirts and 2 choices for pants.
Apply the product rule: Multiply the number of choices for shirts by the number of choices for pants.

blocks.title: Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
blocks.text: The inclusion-exclusion principle is used to count the number of elements in the union of overlapping sets. It states: $|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$, where $|A|$ and $|B|$ are the sizes of sets $A$ and $B$, and $|A \cap B|$ is the size of their intersection.

blocks.title: Using Inclusion-Exclusion
blocks.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 play soccer and 12 play basketball. If 5 students play both sports, how many students play at least one sport?

steps.text: Identify the sizes of the sets: $|A| = 18$, $|B| = 12$, and $|A \cap B| = 5$.

blocks.answer: 25 students play at least one sport.

blocks.title: Pigeonhole Principle
blocks.text: The pigeonhole principle states that if $n$ items are put into $m$ containers, with $n > m$, then at least one container must contain more than one item.

blocks.title: Applying the Pigeonhole Principle
blocks.prompt: Prove that in a group of 13 people, at least two people must have been born in the same month.

steps.text: Identify the number of items and containers: 13 people and 12 months.
Apply the pigeonhole principle: Since there are more people than months, at least one month must have at least two people born in it.

blocks.answer: At least two people were born in the same month.

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text: Counting principles allow us to efficiently determine the number of configurations without exhaustive enumeration. They are foundational for understanding more complex topics in mathematics and computer science.

points: The sum rule is used when choosing between mutually exclusive options.
The product rule is used for sequential choices.
The inclusion-exclusion principle accounts for overlapping sets.
The pigeonhole principle proves existence claims when items outnumber containers.
